newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN details gross rights abuses in Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: UN details gross rights abuses in Nigeria.

text.p: Despite widespread criticisms around the world, Nigeria's military government has done little to stop summary executions, arbitrary arrests and systematic torture of political prisoners, according to a U.N. human rights report released on Monday.

The civilian judicial system barely functions, is short of funds and is riddled with bribes while parallel military tribunals usurp the little authority it has, according to the report for the U.N. General Assembly by two investigators.

The assembly is expected to adopt a critical resolution before the end of the year, thereby diminishing the chance for leadership posts that Nigeria, which is Africa's most populous country, may seek in the United Nations.

The report came from two jurists, called rapporteurs -- Senegal's Bacre Waly Ndiaye and Malaysia's Param Cumaraswany -- who gave a long list of lawyers, journalists, human rights advocates and politicians killed, arrested without trial, tortured in prison or shot while demonstrating peacefully.

For example, Baribo Bera, a member of the Ogoni community detained since 1994 "was reportedly stripped naked, tied to a pillar, flogged with a horsewhip and forced to swallow his teeth that had been knocked out as a result of the beetings."

Some protestors against the government have been killed or beaten up on the street. Those who do land in jails "may be held indefinitely, incommunicado and without opportunity to challenge the legality of their detention," the report said.

Civilian judges sometimes bring in their own paper and pens to record their judgments in underfunded courtrooms. Judges and prosecutors are so poorely paid that "bribery is reported to be a common trend," it added.

But many cases are automatically usurped by parallel military courts, particularly those involving the army itself. And orders from the civilian courts, such as visits to prisoners by lawyers or their families, are routinely ignored by the government, the report said.

Nigeria came under close U.N. scrutiny for its human rights abuses a year ago when the government of military ruler Gen. Sani Abacha aroused world-wide condemnation for spurning appeals for clemency for nine men, including Saro-Wiwa, a respected writer and defender of his own Ogoni minority.

The nine had been found guilty of inciting the murder of four pro-government Ogoni chiefs, but human rights groups saw them as victims of political repression. Nigeria has been subject to a series of sanctions by individual countries, such as an arms embargo, but calls for stiff economic sanctions have not been enacted.

The rapporteurs made a series of recommendations, including investigations of abuses by the military and compensation to its victims. It also said prisoners arbitrarily arrested should be released and the period of pre-trial detention reduced.
